summaries.summary: The introduction opens with the Italian quotation “Ché saetta previsa vien più lenta.”
The quotation is attributed to Dante Alighieri, Divina Commedia, Paradiso.
Antisocial behavior is widespread and potentially damaging online, motivating computational approaches to assist human moderators.
Prior work has focused on post-hoc identification of hate speech, harassment, personal attacks, and general toxicity, limiting pre-emptive moderation.
Forecasting future derailment from early warning signs could enable intervention and belongs to broader conversational forecasting tasks.
Conversational forecasting must model dynamic interactions between comments, beyond individual content, using relations or neural attention architectures.
Unknown conversation horizons complicate forecast timing, while prior fixed-window or event-time assumptions create practical limitations.
The authors introduce an online model processing comments and relations as they happen, inspired by context-aware dialog generation systems.
Adapting generative dialog models to supervised forecasting is difficult because labeled data are scarce, often at most a few thousands examples.
The authors decouple unsupervised pre-training of conversational dynamics from fine-tuned prediction, applying pre-train-then-fine-tune to conversational forecasting.

Two new datasets are developed: an expanded `Conversations Gone Awry' dataset and a ChangeMyView dataset, where the model outperforms baselines and triggers on average 3 comments (or 3 hours) before overt toxicity.
The authors state that they summarize their work.
They introduce the first model for forecasting conversational events that captures dynamics as a conversation develops.
They build two diverse datasets, one entirely new and one extending prior work, for forecasting derailment of online conversations.
They compare their model against the current state-of-the-art and evaluate its ability to provide early warning signs.
The work aims to assist human moderators but cautions that automated systems may encode or amplify training-data biases.
Antisocial behavior online includes harassment, cyberbullying, and general aggression, with prior work studying community effects, actors, and outside-world connections.
Prior post-hoc conversation classification includes debate winners, successful negotiations, deception, and disagreement detection.
The authors instead forecast conversational events before they happen during ongoing conversations, potentially allowing interventions.
Prior conversational forecasting relies on hand-crafted features, whereas the authors aim to learn neural representations through pre-training.
Hand-crafted features typically use fixed-length windows, leaving unknown horizons unaddressed; the authors implement a simple sliding windows baseline.
NLP pre-training commonly uses language modeling objectives, while the authors' conversation-level generative objective is framed as conversational modeling.
Two datasets are considered: an expanded annotated Wikipedia conversations dataset and a secondary ChangeMyView dataset based on future moderator action.
BIBREF9's `Conversations Gone Awry' dataset contains 1,270 Wikipedia Talk Page conversations labeled for personal attacks or civility.
Controls pair attack-containing and clean conversations from the same talk page and ensure comments preceding personal attacks are civil.
The `Conversations Gone Awry' dataset is expanded to 4,188 conversations, focusing on longer conversations with 4 or more comments preceding the attack, and released in ConvoKit.
An 80-20-20 train/dev/test split preserves paired conversations, and another 1 million WikiConv conversations are sampled for unsupervised pre-training.
The CMV dataset uses Reddit API conversations and labels whether a comment was removed for violating Rule 2: “Don't be rude or hostile to other users”.
CMV controls reproduce topic pairing and prior user involvement, yielding 6,842 conversations, an 80-20-20 split, and over 600,000 unlabeled conversations.
CRAFT integrates an unsupervised generative dialog model and a supervised component that fine-tunes the representation to forecast future events.
A conversation is modeled as a sequence of $N$ comments, each represented as a variable-length sequence of $M_n$ tokens.
The generative component uses HRED, a hierarchical recurrent encoder-decoder designed to account for dependencies between consecutive inputs.
An HRED dialog model has an utterance encoder, a context encoder, and a decoder, with the utterance encoder generating semantic comment representations.
The nonlinear gating function uses GRU, and the final hidden state $h^{\text{enc}}_M$ encodes the entire comment.
Running the encoder on each comment produces $N$ vector encodings, over which a second context encoder is run.
Each context hidden state encodes the full conversational context up to comment $n$ and initializes the decoder hidden state for response generation.
The decoder outputs word probabilities, is augmented with attention over context encoder states, and can be pre-trained using unlabeled conversational data.
The predictor is a 3-layer MLP with leaky ReLU and sigmoid output that maps each context encoding to $p_{\text{event}}(c_{n+1})$.
Training initializes encoders from pre-training and computes cross-entropy loss using pre-event contexts for positive samples and full negative contexts.
Fine-tuning allows backpropagation through encoder layers, reshaping the pre-trained representation for prediction.
The model and training code use PyTorch and are publicly released with trained models and data as part of ConvoKit.
CRAFT is evaluated on Wikipedia and CMV derailment forecasting by pre-training on unlabeled data and fine-tuning on labeled training splits.
Comment-level predictions are aggregated using a development-split threshold, with true positives requiring forecasts before actual derailment.
Fixed-length window baselines are Awry, based on pragmatic features in the first comment-reply pair, and BoW using TF-IDF weighted bag-of-words features.
Cumulative BoW recomputes bag-of-words features on all comments seen so far but fails to account for relationships between comments.
Sliding Awry applies Awry features to a window of $W$ comments upon each new comment, with comment-level predictions aggregated as in the main model.
Two CRAFT ablations evaluate the impact of pre-training and hierarchical memory for capturing inter-comment dependencies.
Training CRAFT without pre-training on only labeled data performs at random guessing, underscoring the need for unlabeled-data pre-training.
CRAFT $-$ CE sets context encoder memory size to zero, acting like vanilla seq2seq and predicting only from the latest comment.
Table TABREF17 shows CRAFT outperforms baselines in accuracy and F1 on both datasets, with superior precision-recall balance and larger AUPR on Wikipedia data.
The analysis examines CRAFT’s benefits and limitations, specifically early warning and whether it learns an order-sensitive representation of conversational context.
The analysis asks whether the model triggers early enough to provide pre-emptive, actionable warning to moderators for practical goals.

For correctly forecasted personal attacks, the model warns 3 comments before the attack, 4 comments for CMV, with over 50% of conversations getting at least 3 hours of advance warning, 2 hours for CMV, and 39% getting at least 12 hours.

The analysis asks whether CRAFT uses its capacity for order-sensitive conversational context or computes an order-insensitive “bag-of-features”, using two exploratory experiments despite neural network opacity.

In the prefix-shuffling experiment visualized in Figure FIGREF23, shuffling the first $t-1$ comments changes CRAFT’s prediction in roughly one fifth of cases, 12% for CMV, unlike the Cumulative BoW baseline.
Shuffling comment order in pre-training, fine-tuning and testing hurts performance to 65% accuracy for Wikipedia and 59.5% for CMV, similar to disabling the context encoder.
The experiments provide evidence that CRAFT models conversational context order-sensitively and effectively uses its dynamics, while future work should develop more transparent models.

The work introduced a model for forecasting conversational events that updates predictions at each step, achieves state-of-the-art performance on two publicly released datasets, and can provide substantial prior notice of derailment.
The authors view the work as a step toward real-time forecasting of other emergent conversation properties, with follow-up work adapting CRAFT to other tasks and adding supervised fine-tuning.

Open questions for derailment forecasting concern moderators’ desired warning timing, the optimal balance between precision, recall, and false positive rate, ethical implications, and user studies with actual moderators.
A practical limitation is reliance on balanced datasets, although derailment is rare and $AUPR=0.7$ suggests robustness across thresholds, with more work needed on the recall tradeoff.

A major limitation is assigning a single derailment label to each conversation, while finer-grained forecasting could account for trajectories such as recovery, repeat antisocial behavior, or other paths.
The acknowledgements thank named collaborators and anonymous reviewers, and state support from NSF CAREER award IIS-1750615 and NSF Grant SES-1741441.
